title: Thread-safe event delivery
idea: A thread-safe event bus lets any thread publish or subscribe safely, runs subscribers in parallel, and still delivers events with the same key in order.

analogy.text: A bank assigns each customer a fixed counter. One customer's requests are served in arrival order, while other counters serve other customers at once.
analogy.breaks: An idle counter here cannot take work from a busy one.

points: A shared pool lets a later same-key event overtake an earlier one.
A key lane is one single-thread executor; the key's hash picks the lane.
Different keys usually get different lanes; keys sharing a lane wait their turn.
A `CopyOnWriteArrayList` of subscriptions lets publish iterate while others subscribe.

steps.caption: EV-1 for key O-1 is hashed to a lane. Only that lane's single thread will run it.
EV-2 has the same key, so it lands in the same lane, queued behind EV-1.
EV-3 has key O-2 and another lane. It runs at once, in parallel, without waiting.
EV-1's handler is slow. EV-2 waits, because a lane's one thread works in order.
EV-1 finishes, then EV-2 runs. Billing sees placed before paid on every run.

code.title: Prove the reorder and the fix
code.caption: The first handler waits for the second, so any overtaking shows on every run rather than by luck.

walk.text: Run the same two-event race on a shared pool, then on key lanes.
The placed handler waits up to 500 ms for paid to finish.
Paid records itself and releases the latch; close waits for both.
Shared pool: any idle thread takes the next task, whatever its key.
Key lanes: the key's hash picks one single-thread lane. Paid waits, so placed times out first.

code.title: Subscribe during delivery
code.caption: A handler that subscribes while an event is delivered breaks a plain list but not a copy-on-write one.

walk.text: The welcome handler subscribes a new handler in the middle of delivery.
ArrayList's iterator detects the change and throws on its next step.
CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates a snapshot: no exception, and the late handler waits for the next event.
Four threads subscribe 500 handlers each, and no add is lost.

pitfalls: Do not hand events to a shared pool when consumers need per-key order.
Bound each lane's queue; an unbounded queue hides a slow subscriber until memory runs out.
Use copy-on-write lists only when subscribing is rare and publishing is frequent.

quiz.q: What does KeyedDispatch print for the shared pool?
quiz.why: The pool gives paid to a second thread while placed waits on the latch. Paid records first and releases the latch, then placed records.

takeaway: Hash each key to one lane: parallel across keys, ordered within a key.

starters: How many lanes should a subscriber get in production?
What happens to order if I change the number of lanes at runtime?
Why not use a ReadWriteLock around the subscriber list?
